qt: to the Commission Beatrice Timgren (ECR), Dick Erixon (ECR), Charlie Weimers (ECR) Subject:

The Nature Restoration Regulation requires the restoration of drained peatlands in agricultural use, but permits flexibility when rewetting would have considerable negative consequences for, inter alia, infrastructure, climate adaptation and other public interests.1 A Swedish government report refers to the importance of peat as a growing medium and states that horticultural peat is the dominant raw material for the production of forest plants and that satisfactory substitute materials are not yet available in the volumes and quality that are required for all applications.2 At the same time, the Commission’s own preparedness strategy stresses that disruption in the supply chains for energy, food and critical raw materials can have serious consequences for the Union.3 In light of the above: 1.
How will the Commission ensure that Sweden's restoration plan will not disproportionately reduce the availability of domestically produced horticultural and energy peat?
Does the Commission consider that food supply, energy preparedness and domestic value chains can be covered by ‘other public interests’ in Article 11.4?
Will the Commission take account of the effects on competitiveness, energy preparedness and food chains when it submits views on national measures?

Nature Restoration Regulation, Article 11.4, OJ L, 2024/1991, 29.7.2024. at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.10.2026) The Commission is aware of challenges of replacing peat in some horticultural uses. EU-funded research, such as Horizon 2020 Organic-PLUS1, has examined alternative growing-media components and ways to reduce peat reliance. The Nature Restoration Regulation (NRR)2 does not set targets for peat extraction or production. Article 11(4) requires Member States to restore organic soils in agricultural use constituting drained peatlands (at least 30% by 2030, 40% by 2040 and 50% by 2050) with minimum shares to be rewetted (at least a quarter by 2030 and a third by 2040 and 2050). Peat extraction sites are not subject to these targets, although Member States may choose to restore or rewet them and count them towards the Article 11(4) targets. As outlined in the Vision for agriculture and food3, food production is a key strategic sector for the Union. This is reinforced by Articles 1(1) and 11(1) of the NRR, which acknowledge the importance of food security, rural socio-economic needs and sustainable agricultural production. Under Article 17, the Commission will assess Sweden's draft plan against Articles 15 and 4 to 13 and its contribution to Article 1 objectives. It will consider socio-economic impacts, links with the national energy and climate plan and food security. Synergies between the NRR, the EU Bioeconomy Strategy4 and the potential of the Swedish forestry sector were also highlighted in the Commission reply to written question E-002211/2026.
